newsitem.title: UK: British business gives victorious Labour wish list.
newsitem.headline: British business gives victorious Labour wish list.

text.p: British business groups flocked to congratulate the Labour Party on its landslide election victory on Friday, but were equally quick to present the new government with their own wish lists.
Key lobby groups also called for clarification of important Labour policies now that Tony Blair's reshaped party has ousted the ruling Conservatives.

"The priority now must be to remove the uncertainty surrounding the new government's policies on the single currency, social chapter, minimum wage and the economy," David Richardson, president of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) said.
Concern with Britain's attitude to Europe under the new Labour government was also voiced by other business groups.

The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) said it welcomed Labour's commitments on inflation, personal tax and departmental spending levels as well as improving the education system and its determination to complete the European single market.
"In the areas of policy where we have concerns , the priority is now to ensure the government reflects business interests in the detail of implementation," Adair Turner, CBI director-general said.

Turner highlighted the level of the minimum wage, the extent and nature of Labour's proposed windfall tax on the privatised utilities and the details of trade union recognition proposals as the CBI's main areas of concern.
He said Labour had made its position on many business issues clear, its agenda was well known and CBI members looked forward to working with Tony Blair and his team in government.
But both the CBI and the BCC voiced the European "Social Chapter" as an important concern, raising the possibility of conflict with the incoming government.
Labour has said it will end Britain's opt-out, negotiated by the outgoing Conservatives, from this European framework for minimum working conditions.

In what it called its six-point challenge to Labour, the BCC called on it to "maintain our opt-out from the Social Chapter in order to protect labour market flexibility" while the CBI said "the challenge will be for the government to win the argument in Europe for flexible labour markets and against unnecessary intervention".
The other main points of the BCC challenge were that Labour should take an early decision on whether to join a single European currency in 1999 "based on the best interests of the British economy".
It should use fiscal policy, if necessary adjusting income tax, in order to stave off inflation but avoiding the harm interest rate rises would do to business competitiveness, the BCC added.
The BCC also called on Labour not to establish a minimum wage "at a level which will harm competitiveness and jobs" and to begin a debate on how to tackle Britain's skills deficit.
It also wants Labour to ensure proposals for regional development address issues like transport infrastructure without creating bureaucratic quangos.

The British Retail Consortium (BRC), which says it represents 90 percent of the retail industry by sales, said retailers had an important role to play in the job creation strategies planned by Labour.

"Success will depend on the new government's commitment to a broad economic environment that continues to encourage investment, competition and choice in the High Street," its director general Ann Robinson said.
Britain's Association of Chartered Certified Accountants (ACCA) was also quick to publish what it called its "Ten Commandments for the Labour Government".

Many of its proposals were aimed at small businesses, which it said would expand and "make an even more significant contribution to the economy" if adopted according to ACCA's president Peter Langard.
This focus on small business would also improve employment prospects, Langard said.
